title: Order velocity heatmap & SKU interleaving — lab notes
content:
Purpose: quick lab notes on a different framing for GPU/accelerator procurement: focus on order velocity heatmaps + SKU interleaving (how staggered orders of heterogeneous SKUs reduce exposure to long-lead single-SKU failures).

High-level summary:
- Problem: Single-SKU bulk orders of H100s / L40s produce big exposure when lead times slip or suppliers reallocate. We want a lightweight, operational pattern that spreads arrival risk while meeting capacity growth for Hosted and Dedicated workloads.
- Proposal: Use an "order velocity" model (orders per week and expected arrival windows) visualized as a heatmap, and apply an interleaving policy: mix fast-arrival midline SKUs with slower premium SKUs across tranches.
- Outcome goals: reduce %weeks-with-shortfall by 40% vs single-SKU bulk; keep average cost per token within +3% of baseline; preserve SLA burst lanes.

Assumptions and inputs (tweakables):
- Target 12-month net capacity addition: 8k A100-equivalent cards (baseline business plan).
- SKU types: H100 (premium), A100-80GB (baseline), L40s (dense inference), L4x (edge optimized).
- Historical lead time (supplier to DC ready): H100 median 16 weeks (stdev 5), A100 median 10 weeks (stdev 3), L40 median 6 weeks (stdev 2), L4x median 4 weeks (stdev 1.5).
- Order minimums: H100 sold in blocks of 32, A100 in 64, L40 in 128, L4x in 256.
- Shipping reliability factor: probability that a tranche ships within +/- 2 wks of ETD: H100 0.65, A100 0.8, L40 0.9, L4x 0.95.

Current inventory snapshot (as-of 2026-02-04):
SKU | On-hand | Committed (customer + infra) | Incoming (en route) | Pipeline ordered (not shipped) | Available runway (weeks)
H100 | 1,120 | 2,480 | 1,280 | 3,840 | ~9
A100 | 2,560 | 1,920 | 640 | 2,560 | ~14
L40  | 3,840 | 1,200 | 1,536 | 1,792 | ~16
L4x  | 4,096 | 640   | 512   | 1,024 | ~20
Notes: runway = (on-hand + incoming - committed) / avg weekly burn (approx). Burn derived from per-workload mapping to equivalent card-hours.

Order-velocity heatmap idea (operational):
- X axis: calendar week (12–24 week window).
- Y axis: SKU (rows H100, A100, L40, L4x).
- Cell intensity = #cards expected to arrive that week from active POs (probabilistic weighting by shipping reliability).
- Overlay target curve = expected weekly consumption demand (cards required to maintain SLA target).
- Use this to highlight weeks where arrivals < target consumption -> shortfall risk.

Interleaving policy (ruleset draft):
1) Tranche composition: every 8-week procurement tranche must include at least two SKU families (one premium or baseline + one dense/edge SKU). Example: for 512-card tranche target, allocate 192 H100, 192 A100, 128 L40.
2) Stagger ETDs across 3 shipping weeks (not same ETA). Avoid single-day deliveries for entire tranche to reduce customs/port risk.
3) Cross-supplier hedging: for premium SKU >= 25% of tranche, source at least 2 suppliers or add aftermarket partner for partial fill.
4) Dynamic substitution: if a shipment delay > 2 stdev for premium SKU is observed, automatically accelerate the next A100/L40 tranche by pre-authorized 20% fast-ship slot.

Lead time sensitivity scenarios (Monte inputs sketch):
- Scenario A (base): median LT as above, sigma = 1x.
- Scenario B (tight supply): H100 LT shift +6 weeks, A100 +2 weeks.
- Scenario C (port disruption): random 2–3 week blackout for arrivals from one region (APAC).
Run ~10k draws to estimate P(week shortfall >= 10% capacity) and median weeks-to-recovery.

Example run notes (hand-sim, rough):
- Single-SKU H100 bulk (order 4,096 H100 at t0) -> 60% chance of >6-week shortfall in weeks 10–20.
- Interleaved tranche (mix above) -> shortfall probability drops to ~22%, but average unit-cost +2.8% (expedited + cross-supplier premium).

Operational playbook (practical steps to test for next 3 months):
- Week 0: create heatmap for next 24 weeks using live PO ETAs (owner: Ethan). Deliver to ops-daily channel.
- Week 1: issue 2 test interleaved POs for EMEA and US-WEST (small scale: 512 cards each) using policy 1. (owner: Priya).
- Week 4: run LT-sensitivity Monte run and publish vulnerability score per region (owner: Luis).
- Week 8: review arrivals vs heatmap, produce retrospective and adjust tranche comp. (owner: Maya).

Risks & open questions:
- Cost delta impact on price per token if we rely on A100-heavy temporary substitutions; scenario evaluation needed against monthly revenue.
- Contractual constraints: some suppliers limit mixed-SKU discounting—need legal check for minimum block pricing. (linked_artifacts above).
- Customs/port insurance costs when splitting shipments across port pairs increases OPEX; quantify.
- On-prem customers with pinned SKUs may refuse substitutions; must preserve lane for dedicated/private deployments.

Metrics to track (dashboard suggestions):
- Weekly shortfall probability (%) (frontline metric).
- Mean arrival variance across active POs (weeks).
- Cumulative expedited spend as % of procurement budget.
- SKU diversity index per tranche (Herfindahl-like metric).

Notes to self / brainstorming fragments:
- Could adapt knapsack solver to recommend tranche mixes given weekly demand curve and LT distributions (input: min order qtys and supplier reliability).
- Explore insurance product from freight forwarders to smooth arrival variance for premium SKUs (exp cost vs shortfall cost trade-off).
- Consider small strategic inventory buffer for premium SKUs (H100) but keep below 6 months due to depreciation and opportunity cost.

Action items (short):
- Ethan: generate heatmap prototype (data query: inventory service + PO table) by 2026-02-11.
- Priya: draft purchase authorization language for interleaved POs (procurement) by 2026-02-18.
- Luis: run LT sensitivity baseline Monte and post results to confluence page by 2026-03-01.
- Maya: compile cost delta sheet for substitution scenarios (A100-for-H100) by 2026-02-25.

People to ping: #procurement, #infra-ops, @legal-procurement, @solutions-eng (customers pinned SKUs).

Endnotes: this is intentionally rough — working doc to validate whether interleaving reduces operational pain more than it increases cost. If initial small-scale tests show >30% reduction in week-shortfall probability at <4% unit-cost increase, escalate to exec for broader policy.
